_note: Example output produced by IncidentIQ from the input files in this same folder (examples/checkout-v2.4.1). Model output is not deterministic; a fresh run may differ in wording and confidence values.

summary.summary: Checkout service v2.4.1 was deployed at 14:05 and passed health checks. Roughly seven minutes later, at 14:12, payment finalisation began timing out and POST /api/checkout started returning 500s, with the service reporting its database connection pool exhausted at 20/20. At the same moment orders-db reported reaching its ceiling of max_connections=100, while an unrelated reporting service held 74 idle connections to the same database. Errors continued past 14:16, after autoscaling raised checkout from 6 to 10 replicas.

facts.statement: checkout-svc v2.4.1 deployed at 14:05:02 with 6 replicas and all pods passed health checks by 14:05:40.
facts.evidence: 14:05:02 deploy checkout-svc image=checkout:2.4.1 replicas=6 OK / 14:05:40 healthcheck /healthz 200

facts.statement: The first checkout 500 errors appear at 14:12:03, about seven minutes after the deploy completed.
facts.evidence: 14:12:03 ERROR checkout-svc POST /api/checkout 500 (orders-db pool exhausted: 20/20 in use)

facts.statement: orders-db reached its configured ceiling of 100 active connections at 14:12:09.
facts.evidence: 14:12:09 ERROR orders-db too many connections (max_connections=100, active=100)

facts.statement: reporting-svc held 74 idle connections to orders-db at 14:12:10.
facts.evidence: 14:12:10 WARN reporting-svc opened 74 idle connections to orders-db

facts.statement: Release v2.4.1 raised the checkout connection pool from 10 to 20 per pod and contained no schema changes.
facts.evidence: Deployment notes: raised DB connection pool per pod from 10 -> 20; No schema changes.

facts.statement: The autoscaler increased checkout from 6 to 10 replicas at 14:15, and errors continued at 14:16:41.

assumptions.statement: All six checkout pods were requesting close to their full pool of 20 connections.
assumptions.why: Only one pod's exhaustion is logged; the input never states per-pod connection counts, so the 6x20=120 figure is inferred, not measured.

assumptions.statement: The reporting-svc export job began its run at 14:00.
assumptions.why: The deployment note says it runs at :00 of each hour, but the only evidence of connections is a single line at 14:12:10.

assumptions.statement: checkout-svc and reporting-svc are the main consumers of orders-db.
assumptions.why: The input does not enumerate every service connecting to this database, so other consumers may exist.

assumptions.statement: Customers reporting a charge without confirmation were actually charged.
assumptions.why: Six support tickets describe this, but no payment-provider record appears in the input to confirm it.

hypotheses.title: Combined connection demand exceeded the shared orders-db ceiling of 100
supporting: orders-db explicitly reports max_connections=100 with active=100 at 14:12:09
checkout alone could request 6 pods x 20 = 120 connections after v2.4.1, already above the ceiling
reporting-svc simultaneously held 74 idle connections to the same database
Failures are connection timeouts and pool exhaustion, not application exceptions
contradicting: Only one pod's pool exhaustion is logged; actual per-service connection counts are not in the input
The seven-minute gap between deploy and first error is unexplained by this hypothesis alone
hypotheses.test: Query pg_stat_activity grouped by application_name during a reproduction and compare the real per-service totals against 100.

hypotheses.title: The reporting-svc hourly export is the dominant consumer of the connection budget
supporting: 74 of the 100 available connections were held by reporting-svc
The job was deployed only today at 09:30, making it a recent change to the shared database
Idle connections consume the ceiling without doing useful work
contradicting: If the job runs hourly at :00, the 12:00 and 13:00 runs presumably did not cause an incident — though the input contains no evidence either way
Errors began at 14:12, not at 14:00 when the job would have started
hypotheses.test: Check connection counts during the 12:00 and 13:00 export runs; if they also approached the ceiling, the deploy is what pushed it over.

hypotheses.title: Autoscaling amplified an already-saturated connection pool
supporting: Replicas rose from 6 to 10 at 14:15, raising potential demand to 200 connections
Errors persist at 14:16:41, after scaling completed
contradicting: The first errors at 14:12:03 predate the scaling event at 14:15:00, so this cannot be the initial cause
At best this is an amplifier, not a root cause
hypotheses.test: Cap replicas or lower the per-pod pool and observe whether the error rate falls while load stays constant.

hypotheses.title: A code defect in v2.4.1 unrelated to connection handling
supporting: Errors began after the v2.4.1 deploy and not before
contradicting: Every error message names connection timeouts or pool exhaustion, not an application fault
All pods passed health checks at 14:05:40
The deployment notes record no schema or logic changes beyond the pool size
hypotheses.test: Deploy v2.4.1 to staging against a dedicated database with a generous connection limit and run a load test.

risks.where: The deploy at 14:05 preceded the errors at 14:12, which makes it tempting to conclude the deploy caused them. The limit actually hit is a shared database ceiling that the deploy only contributed to.
risks.mitigation: Require a stated mechanism connecting cause to effect, not just chronological order, before accepting any hypothesis.

risks.where: The PagerDuty alert names checkout, so attention anchors on the checkout service and its recent release rather than on the shared database.
risks.mitigation: Enumerate every consumer of orders-db before naming a cause; the alert names the victim, not necessarily the culprit.

risks.where: A novel bug in v2.4.1 feels like a satisfying explanation, but shared-resource exhaustion is a far more common production failure mode.
risks.mitigation: Rank ordinary causes such as connection limits, disk, and memory before exotic ones, and require stronger evidence for the exotic.

risks.where: Once the pool-exhaustion story is favoured, the reporting-svc line reads as confirmation while the unexplained seven-minute delay gets ignored.
risks.mitigation: Actively search for evidence that would disprove the leading hypothesis, and record it in the contradicting column.

risks.where: This analysis is machine-generated and reads with more authority than its evidence supports; several figures here are inferred rather than measured.
risks.mitigation: Treat every number not traceable to a log line as an assumption, and confirm it before acting.

actions.action: Add an alert on orders-db connection utilisation with a threshold below 100 so the ceiling is visible before it is reached.
actions.link: Prevents recurrence; the incident surfaced only once the limit was already hit

questions: What were the actual per-service connection counts at 14:12? The input gives a figure only for reporting-svc.
Did the 12:00 and 13:00 export runs also elevate connection counts without causing a visible incident?
What is the sum of all configured connection pools across every service pointing at orders-db?
Were payments captured for the checkouts that returned 500, and how many customers are affected?
Why did errors begin at 14:12 rather than immediately after the 14:05 deploy?

devil.counter: The seven-minute gap between a completed deploy and the first error is the weakest point in the leading hypothesis, and nothing in the evidence explains it.
points: If 6 pods x 20 connections truly exceeded the ceiling on their own, saturation should have appeared within seconds of the pods becoming ready at 14:05:40, not seven minutes later.

The 74 idle connections from reporting-svc are recorded at 14:12:10 — one second after the ceiling was already reported. That ordering is consistent with reporting-svc being a symptom of a stalled database rather than the cause of the saturation.
No baseline is available. We do not know what normal connection usage looks like, so we cannot say the observed numbers are abnormal rather than typical for this hour.

A traffic spike at 14:12 driven by something entirely outside this data — a marketing send, a bot, a retry storm from an upstream client — would produce exactly these symptoms with or without the deploy.
devil.blindspot: Committing now means treating the deploy and the reporting job as the whole story, and never checking whether an external traffic change at 14:12 was the actual trigger. The absence of request-rate data in the input is the largest gap in this investigation.

audit.note: The pool size of 20 and the replica count of 6 are both in the input, but no line shows all pods holding full pools. The product is arithmetic, not evidence.
